(6) An action-outcome repertoire: representing a hierarchical skill library Channel capacity depends critically on the size and structure of the input "alphabet"–the set of distinguishable actions the agent can emit. Empowerment computation therefore requires the agent to maintain an inventory of its available action primitives and, crucially, to represent which actions are functionally distinct in their state-space consequences (since two motor commands that produce identical outcomes contribute nothing to channel capacity). This connects empowerment to the concept of option discovery in reinforcement learning 1: acquiring new temporally extended action primitives (options, skills, macro-actions) that produce reliably distinct outcomes effectively increases the alphabet size of the control channel, directly boosting the achievable empowerment. On this view, skill acquisition is channel expansion: each new reliably executable skill adds a new "symbol" to the action alphabet, increasing ℰ\mathcal{E} by enabling the agent to reach states that were previously inaccessible or indistinguishable. The hierarchical organization of motor control–from low-level muscle synergies to high-level action plans 2–can then be understood as a multi-resolution encoding of the action channel: low-level primitives provide fine-grained but local controllability, while high-level skills ("go to the kitchen," "build a shelter") provide coarse but far-reaching causal influence over temporally distant states, and empowerment at different planning horizons kk is maximized by operating at the appropriate level of the hierarchy.

Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior?

The brain’s action repertoire is organized as a genetically scaffolded hierarchy of motor representations, each level contributing a distinct "alphabet layer" to the control channel. At the base, spinal central pattern generators (CPGs) and brainstem motor nuclei define a set of phylogenetically ancient, largely innate motor primitives–locomotor rhythms, postural synergies, orofacial patterns, reaching-and-grasping coordination–that constitute the organism’s factory-installed action alphabet 3, 4.

Muscle synergies–low-dimensional patterns of co-activation across muscles that can be recombined to produce a wide range of behaviors–provide one influential description of this compression: many natural motor outputs can be approximated by combinations of a modest set of such patterns rather than independent control of each muscle 5. However, the extent to which synergies should be interpreted as discrete, hardwired control "units" versus emergent regularities shaped by biomechanics, task constraints, and learning remains an active debate; a conservative statement is that early spinal/brainstem circuitry provides strong structural constraints on coordination, while development, exploration, and practice refine and reshape the effective basis over time 4, 5. Thus, the channel’s lowest-level "alphabet" is available very early, but it is not purely fixed: it is progressively tuned by experience as cortical and subcortical learning systems come online 3, 4. A 2026 computational study models learning muscle synergies (Figure) 33. The model tracks changes in simulated synergies (Figure).

Above this base layer, primary motor cortex (M1) and a premotor/medial motor hierarchy (PMd, PMv, SMA, pre-SMA) participate in control at longer timescales and higher levels of abstraction, as established by genetically specified areal boundaries, laminar connectivity motifs, and corticospinal projection patterns 6, 7. While the precise mapping is not strictly one-to-one (each area is multifunctional and highly interactive), a broadly supported functional division is: M1 is most tightly linked to movement execution and relatively fine-grained parameters (force, velocity, direction for specific effectors); dorsal/ventral premotor areas (PMd/PMv) contribute to action preparation and selection in terms of goals, targets, and grasp/hand configurations (actions in the behavioral rather than muscular sense); SMA is especially implicated in internally generated actions and the organization/ordering of learned action sequences; and pre-SMA and rostral prefrontal areas are more strongly recruited when selecting or switching action sets under abstract task demands ("which kind of action policy to engage") 6, 7. In this framing, each level provides a progressively more abstract "alphabet" (from fast coordination patterns to action plans to sequence structure to task-level control), and higher-level selections bias and constrain lower-level motor release through dense corticocortical and cortico-subcortical interactions rather than a purely serial top-down chain 6, 7. A 2026 mouse study records motor-cortical interneurons during action learning (Figure) 34.

A key mechanism for effective channel expansion–in the sense of creating new, distinguishable, reusable action units that can be selected as if they were single primitives at a higher temporal grain–is action-sequence chunking in dorsal striatum (dorsolateral striatum in rodents; putamen in primates). With repetition, cortico-striatal circuits come to treat a multi-element sequence as a unitized behavioral object: neural activity in sensorimotor striatum evolves from broadly tracking many elements to exhibiting characteristic boundary or "bracketing” signals (selective responses at sequence initiation/termination), consistent with a learned delimiter-like representation of the chunk 8, 9, 10. This phenomenon is strongly dopamine-linked, reinforcing the view that chunk formation is shaped by reinforcement-modulated plasticity in BG loops 9, 11, 12. Functionally, once a sequence is chunked it can be gated, competed over, and released by cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry more like a single temporally extended action than a chain that must be re-planned element-by-element 13, 8. This is the neural instantiation of skill acquisition as channel expansion–each consolidated chunk adds a new entry to the action alphabet at its hierarchical level, enabling causal influence over more temporally distant states without requiring step-by-step planning through the primitive action space. The study examines learning of a longer action sequence (Figure). A 2025 mouse study tests the tail of the striatum in action learning (Figure) 35. The study tests whether tail-striatal dopamine reinforces state–action associations (Figure).

Cerebellar learning plays a complementary role. The cerebellum is strongly implicated in acquiring and refining predictive internal models (forward/inverse computations) that support fast, low-latency, feedforward calibration of movement dynamics and error-based fine-tuning of execution 14, 15. In human sequence-skill learning, extended practice often shows a network reweighting in which early learning recruits cerebellar-cortical components more strongly, whereas later, well-learned performance increasingly engages sensorimotor putamen/striatum and shows reduced cerebellar cortical involvement (with phase-dependent changes in deep cerebellar contributions), consistent with a division of labor: BG contributes to selection/serialization and chunk-level control, while cerebellar circuitry supports predictive execution and refinement 16, 17, 18. On evolutionary timescales, the disproportionate expansion of the cerebellum in anthropoid primates and especially humans is well supported, and this expansion includes cerebellar regions coupled to prefrontal systems rather than being purely "motor" 19, 20. A conservative interpretation consistent with these data is that cerebellar enlargement reflects an evolutionary investment in scalable predictive modeling and automatization across large repertoires of sensorimotor (and likely cognitive) skills–increasing the brain’s capacity to deploy well-calibrated, rapidly executable control policies once they are learned, while BG loops remain available for continued acquisition and selection of new chunked action structures 15, 20. A developmental experiment measures reaching adaptation (Figure) 36. The study compares adaptation across age groups (Figure).

For empowerment, what matters is not the raw cardinality of the motor command set, but the functional discriminability of actions in their induced outcome distributions–i.e., whether different actions lead to reliably distinguishable future sensory states. This follows directly from the definition of empowerment as a channel capacity between actions and future states: actions that induce the same (or highly overlapping) conditional outcome distribution contribute little new information, whereas actions that induce separable outcome distributions increase the effective capacity of the action-outcome channel 21, 22, 23.

A plausible neural substrate for tracking this discriminability is the brain’s system for action-effect bindings (ideomotor "event files"): actions are represented together with their anticipated sensory consequences, enabling selection and learning in terms of what an action will cause rather than only the motor command itself 24, 25, 26. Consistent with this framing, frontoparietal planning circuits can encode actions in terms of their expected/desired sensory outcomes: both posterior parietal cortex and dorsal premotor cortex carry information about the visual consequences of upcoming actions during preparation, and intraparietal regions are recruited when action preparation is organized around explicit effect representations 27, 28, 29. The event-file design shows how action–outcome bindings are tested (Figure). The planning contrasts connect action preparation with represented outcomes (Figure).

In this view, two actions that are predicted (in a given context) to yield indistinguishable outcomes will be informationally redundant at the level of empowerment, even if their motor commands differ, because they map to overlapping outcome codes; conversely, a newly acquired skill that produces a reliably novel outcome distribution effectively adds a new distinguishable action-outcome mapping and thus increases the channel’s effective alphabet at that abstraction level 21, 27. Posterior parietal cortex (especially intraparietal sulcus) is well positioned for this computation because it lies at the convergence of sensory state representations and motor-intention/planning signals, and is centrally implicated in parietal-frontal circuits for intention, sensorimotor decision-making, and state estimation–the kinds of representations needed to evaluate the diversity/structure of the action→\rightarrowoutcome mapping that governs channel capacity 30, 31, 32.

The evolutionary architectural priors for the action-outcome repertoire are therefore: (i) spinal CPGs and brainstem nuclei providing a (more or less) genetically specified base alphabet of motor primitives and synergies; (ii) the cortical motor hierarchy (M1→\rightarrowPMd/SMA→\rightarrowpre-SMA→\rightarrowPFC) establishing a graded abstraction axis with genetically specified areal differentiation and hierarchical connectivity; (iii) the parallel CBGTC loop architecture supporting simultaneous maintenance and competitive selection of action repertoires at multiple temporal scales; (iv) cortico-striatal chunking plasticity rules (dopamine-gated Hebbian learning at cortico-striatal synapses) enabling experiential expansion of the alphabet through sequence consolidation; (v) massive cerebellar circuitry for automating consolidated skills and thereby freeing BG capacity for continued hierarchical repertoire growth; and (vi) premotor-parietal action-effect binding networks that track the functional discriminability of the repertoire. The organism is thus born not with a fixed action alphabet but with an expandable, hierarchically organized channel architecture whose initial symbols are genetically installed (reflexes, synergies, CPGs) and whose capacity for alphabet growth–the rate and depth at which new skills can be chunked, consolidated, and stacked–is itself the key evolutionary prior that determines the ceiling on achievable empowerment across the lifespan.
